blocks.text: 1.1.1 Recognition of Real and Imaginary Parts

Is sabaq mein hum seekhenge ke kisi bhi complex number mein real part kaun sa hai aur imaginary part kaun sa, aur conjugate (jora / ulta sign wala saathi) kaise likhte hain. Pichle sabaq mein aap ne dekha tha ke complex number \(a + ib\) ki shakal ka hota hai; ab hum is ke hisson ko naam denge. Yeh chhota sa sabaq hai, lekin poori unit mein har sawal isi pehchan se shuru hoga, is liye ise pakka kar lijiye.

Chaliye ek equation se shuru karte hain aur dekhte hain ke \(i\) kahan se aata hai. Equation \(x^2 + 1 = 0\) ko hum aam tareeqe se hal karte hain: \(1\) ko doosri taraf le jayein, phir dono taraf square root lein:

\[x^2 + 1 = 0\]
\[\Rightarrow x^2 = -1\]
\[\Rightarrow x = \pm\sqrt{-1}\]

Yahan ruk kar dekhiye: jawab \(\sqrt{-1}\) aaya, jo real numbers ke set mein nahi aata, kyunke kisi bhi real number ka square negative nahi hota. To kya hum keh dein ke equation ka koi hal nahi? Mathematicians ne aisa nahi kiya. Aasani ke liye unhon ne \(\sqrt{-1}\) ko imaginary number (khayali number) ka naam diya aur ise \(i\) se likha, jise "iota" parhte hain. Ab \(x^2 + 1 = 0\) ke do jawab hain: \(x = i\) aur \(x = -i\).

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Har real number bhi complex number hai, jis ka imaginary part 0 hota hai.

Ab hisson ke naam. Complex number \(z = a + ib\) mein \(a\) ko real part aur \(b\) ko imaginary part kehte hain. Short mein inhein \(a = \operatorname{Re} z\) aur \(b = \operatorname{Im} z\) likhte hain ("Re" real ka aur "Im" imaginary ka chhota naam hai). Misaal: agar \(z = 3 + 4i\) ho to \(\operatorname{Re} z = 3\) aur \(\operatorname{Im} z = 4\).

Isi tarah kisi non-zero real number \(b\) aur \(i\) ka product (hasil-e-zarb) bhi imaginary number hota hai aur ise \(bi\) (ya \(ib\)) likhte hain. Is tarah \(2i\), \(-3i\), \(\sqrt{5}\,i\), \(-\frac{11}{2}i\) sab isi qisam ke imaginary numbers hain. In sab mein real part zero hai; sirf \(i\) wala hissa mojood hai.

blocks.title: Kitab ki ghalti
blocks.text: Kitab mein chhapa hai ke yeh product "is written as 1", jo ghalat (chhapai ki ghalti) hai. Non-zero real number \(b\) aur \(i\) ka product \(bi\) (ya \(ib\)) likha jata hai, jaise kitab ki apni misalein \(2i\), \(-3i\), \(\sqrt{5}\,i\), \(-\frac{11}{2}i\) saaf dikhati hain.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Ek baat zehan mein achhi tarah bitha lijiye: imaginary part real number \(b\) hai, \(ib\) nahi. \(z = 3 + 4i\) ka \(\operatorname{Im} z = 4\) hai, \(4i\) nahi. Imtihan mein yahan bohat se students number kat-wa lete hain. Sochiye, naam "imaginary part" hai, lekin woh khud ek real number hai jo \(i\) ke saath laga hota hai.
Ab do khaas soorten (special cases) dekhiye:
Agar \(b = 0\) ho to \(z = a + 0i = a\), yani aam real number. Isi liye upar wala Note kehta hai ke har real number complex number bhi hai.
Agar \(a = 0\) aur \(b \ne 0\) ho to \(z = ib\), jaise \(2i\) ya \(-3i\). Ise (purely) imaginary number kehte hain.
Yun samjhiye ke real numbers ek chhota ghar hain jo complex numbers ke bare ghar ke andar bana hua hai: \(\mathbb{R} \subset C\). Har real number complex hai, lekin har complex number real nahi.

blocks.title: Khud sochiye
blocks.text: \(z = -6 + 0i\) ka real part aur imaginary part kya hain? Aur \(z = -\frac{1}{2}i\) ke? Jawab: pehle mein \(\operatorname{Re} z = -6\), \(\operatorname{Im} z = 0\) (yeh real number hai). Doosre mein \(\operatorname{Re} z = 0\), \(\operatorname{Im} z = -\frac{1}{2}\) (yeh purely imaginary hai).
Conjugate Complex Numbers

Ab ek bohat kaam ki cheez seekhte hain: conjugate. Pehle yeh samajh lein ke is ki zaroorat kyun hai. Aage chal kar jab hum complex numbers ki taqseem (division) karenge, ya modulus nikaalenge, to har jagah conjugate hi kaam aayega, kyunke kisi number ko us ke conjugate se zarb dein to \(i\) ghayab ho jata hai aur real number bachta hai.

Definition: agar \(z = a + ib\) ek complex number ho to \(a - ib\) ko \(a + ib\) ka complex conjugate kehte hain, aur ise \(\overline{z}\) (parhte hain "z bar") se likhte hain. Misaal: \(5 + 4i\) complex conjugate hai \(5 - 4i\) ka, aur \(-2 - 3i\) complex conjugate hai \(-2 + 3i\) ka.

blocks.title: Kitab ki ghalti
blocks.text: Kitab mein chhapa hai ke "\(5 - 4i\) is complex conjugate of \(5 - 4i\)". Yeh ghalat hai, kyunke koi number apna conjugate tabhi hota hai jab woh real ho. \(5 - 4i\) ke imaginary part ka sign badlein to \(5 + 4i\) milta hai. Sahi baat: \(5 + 4i\) complex conjugate hai \(5 - 4i\) ka (aur \(5 - 4i\) complex conjugate hai \(5 + 4i\) ka).

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Real number apna conjugate khud hota hai (self-conjugate).

blocks.text_alt: if z equals a plus i b, then z bar equals a minus i b

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Conjugate likhne ka tareeqa bas itna hai: real part waisa hi rehne dijiye, sirf imaginary part ka sign ulta kar dijiye. Plus ho to minus, minus ho to plus.
Ise aaine (mirror) ki tarah samjhiye: agar real axis ek jheel ka kinara ho to \(\overline{z}\) us jheel ke paani mein \(z\) ka aks (reflection) hai. Yeh aap Argand diagram (1.1.5) mein khud dekhenge.
Real number self-conjugate kyun hai? Real number \(a\) asal mein \(a + 0i\) hai. Is ka conjugate \(a - 0i = a\), yani wohi number. Sign badalne ke liye imaginary part hi zero hai, to kuch nahi badalta.
Do dafa conjugate lein to wapas wohi number milta hai: \(\overline{\overline{z}} = z\). Aaine mein aks ka aks, asal cheez hi hoti hai.

blocks.title: Hamari taraf se misaal
blocks.text:
Dekhiye ke conjugate se zarb dene par \(i\) kaise ghayab hota hai. \(z = 3 + 4i\) lijiye, to \(\overline{z} = 3 - 4i\):
\[(3 + 4i)(3 - 4i) = 9 - 16i^2\]
\[= 9 + 16 = 25\]
Jawab mein koi \(i\) nahi, sirf real number 25. Yahi chaal aage division mein istemaal hogi.

blocks.caption: Real part, imaginary part aur conjugate (hamara bana hua table)

blocks.text: Table ko line ba line dekhiye. Har line mein real part waisa hi conjugate mein chala gaya hai, aur sirf \(i\) wale hisse ka sign badla hai. Aakhri do lines par khaas dhyan dein: \(5\) real number hai, is liye us ka conjugate bhi \(5\) hai; aur \(2i\) ka real part zero hai, is liye conjugate \(-2i\) hai.

blocks.title: Yaad rakhne wali baatein
blocks.text:
1. \(i = \sqrt{-1}\) (iota) ko imaginary unit kehte hain.
2. \(z = a + ib\) ke liye \(\operatorname{Re} z = a\) aur \(\operatorname{Im} z = b\); dono real numbers hain.
3. Har real number complex number hai jis ka imaginary part 0 hai.
4. \(\overline{a + ib} = a - ib\): sirf imaginary part ka sign badalta hai, real part wahi rehta hai.
5. Real number apna conjugate khud hai, aur \(\overline{\overline{z}} = z\).

blocks.title: Aam ghaltiyan
blocks.text:
\(\operatorname{Im}(3 + 4i) = 4i\) likhna. Sahi jawab \(4\) hai; \(i\) imaginary part mein shamil nahi.
Conjugate mein dono sign badal dena: \(\overline{3 + 4i} = -3 - 4i\) ghalat hai; sahi \(3 - 4i\) hai. Real part ko haath mat lagaiye.
Minus sign bhool jana: \(2 - \frac{5}{7}i\) mein \(\operatorname{Im} z = -\frac{5}{7}\) hai, \(\frac{5}{7}\) nahi. Sign hamesha number ke saath jata hai.
Yeh samajhna ke conjugate mein sirf "minus laga dena" hai: \(\overline{-2 - 3i}\) ka jawab \(-2 + 3i\) hai, yani yahan minus plus ban gaya.
